Dạng TRUE / FALSE / NOT GIVEN đánh vào đ:
TRUE / FALSE / NOT GIVEN questions target learners' habit of guessing.

TRUE means the passage states it. FALSE means the passage states the opposite. NOT GIVEN means the passage doesn't mention it at all, even if it might be true in real life.

Tip: ask yourself "which line in the passage says this?". If you can point to a specific line, choose TRUE or FALSE. If you have to infer using outside knowledge, the answer is almost certainly NOT GIVEN. A common trap is comparison: the passage says "A is popular" and "B is popular", while the question says "A is more popular than B". The passage never compares them, so the answer is NOT GIVEN.

Học \"make\" riêng và \"decision\" riêng:
If you learn "make" and "decision" separately, you might still blurt out "do a decision" when speaking. Learn the phrase "make a decision" directly and you'll never get it wrong.

Whenever you encounter a new word, write down the whole sentence containing it instead of just the word. For example, instead of writing "reduce: giảm", write "reduce traffic in the city centre: giảm kẹt xe ở trung tâm". In the exam room, the whole phrase will come out naturally.

Pick just five phrases a day, but actually use them. Write your own sentence with each phrase, then read it aloud. Five usable phrases are worth more than fifty words sitting idle in a notebook.

When asked unexpectedly, your mind often goes blank. A simple framework fixes this: main point, reason, example.

For example, with "Do you like cooking?". Main point: "Yes, I really enjoy it." Reason: "because it helps me relax after work." Example: "Last weekend I made beef noodle soup for my family and it took me almost three hours."

Those three sentences are long enough for Part 1 and sound very natural. The key is you don't need brilliant ideas—just think in order. Practice this framework ten times with ten different questions; it will become a reflex and you'll stop fearing awkward silences.

Nhiều bạn nghe một lần rồi cố hiểu hết,:
Many learners listen once and try to understand everything, which only gets more confusing. Split it into two listens with different goals.

On the first listen, don't try to catch every word. Just grasp the context: who is speaking, where they are, and what they want. If you hear "How can I help you?", it's almost certainly a service situation, and the next lines will involve booking, buying, or complaining.

On the second listen, catch the details: numbers, proper names, dates, and times. Before pressing play, read the questions and underline keywords. If a question asks "How much does it cost?", just listen for numbers with pounds, dollars, or the phrase "that comes to". This helps you answer correctly without needing to understand every word.

Task 2 isn't graded on length, but on organization. The safest structure is four paragraphs.

Paragraph one: paraphrase the prompt in your own words and state your opinion. Paragraph two: one main idea with explanation and example. Paragraph three: your second main idea, same structure. Paragraph four: restate your opinion in one sentence.

Each body paragraph should have only one idea. Cramming two ideas into one paragraph is a common mistake that lowers your Coherence score. Leave a blank line between paragraphs—examiners grade quickly and need to see your layout immediately. And always count your words: under 250 will be penalized, no matter how good the essay is.

Ở band 5, ba lỗi này lặp đi lặp lại và k:
At band 5, these three mistakes keep repeating and drag your score down more than you think.

First, missing the third-person s: "He go to work" instead of "He goes to work". Second, forgetting articles: "I am student" instead of "I am a student". Third, mixing up tenses when telling a story: starting in the past and switching to the present halfway through.

The fix isn't learning more theory—it's proofreading. After writing a paragraph, reread it solely to catch these three errors, one at a time. Do this for about two weeks and your fingers will type them right automatically.
